terms.comment: Classically charcoal, dead or glowing: the Romans heated and cooked with wood and charcoal. Modern Latin uses the word for coal too; where it matters, add fossilis.
Our phrase, after Varro’s sāl fossilis, rock salt, and Pliny’s ebur fossile (Lewis & Short, s.v. fossilis, “dug up”). None of the reference works has a word for mineral coal.
Traupman’s word for coal; but gagātēs is jet, a hard black stone (Plin. NH 36.141, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: in vīllā, cum pluet, circumīre oportet, sīcubi perpluat, et signāre carbōne, cum dēsierit pluere, utī tēgula mūtētur
phrases.english: when it rains, you should go round the house to see where the rain comes through, and mark the place with charcoal, so that the tile can be changed when the rain stops
